header: Nonvanishing — the arrow of O67's conditional theorem, in the house pattern. `papers/The-Four-Zeros.md` § I states: under RH, `cell(r,d) ≠ 0` for every `r ≥ R(d)`, which with O43's census makes the four zeros complete at every depth `d ≤ 15`. The proof has two analytic inputs and one arithmetic gap condition; everything joining them is algebra. Following `Chain.lean`'s design — take the antecedents as HYPOTHESES, prove the arrows, let the kernel check that the "therefore" is real — this module proves the joins:

decls.name: bdiffZ
decls.why: Backward differencing on ℤ-indexed real sequences — `Chain.bdiff`'s twin one level down (ℤ index, ℝ values).

decls.name: stencilR
decls.why: The real alternating binomial stencil of order `n` on `g`, read at `r` downward. The ℝ twin of `Zeros.stencil`.

decls.name: iter_bdiffZ_eq_fwdDiff
decls.why: Backward differencing is `(−1)·fwdDiff` at step `−1` — the ℝ copy of `Zeros.tableFrom_eq_fwdDiff`'s bridge.
decls.proves: (bdiffZ^[n]) g r = (-1 : ℝ) ^ n * (fwdDiff (-1 : ℤ))^[n] g r

decls.name: iter_bdiffZ_eq_stencilR
decls.why: `n` differences are the stencil. `Zeros.tableFrom_eq_stencil` transplanted to ℝ: Mathlib's `fwdDiff_iter_eq_sum_shift` does the binomial bookkeeping.
decls.proves: (bdiffZ^[n]) g r = stencilR n g r

decls.name: stencilR_row
decls.why: The Pascal step. The depth-`d` stencil on the row `x ↦ g(x) − g(x−1)` is the depth-`(d+1)` stencil on `g`. One more iterate, nothing else.
decls.proves: stencilR d (bdiffZ g) r = stencilR (d + 1) g r

decls.name: stencilR_sub
decls.why: Linearity. Splitting `π = li + (π − li)` under the stencil.
decls.proves: stencilR n (fun x => f x - L x) r = stencilR n f r - stencilR n L r

decls.name: Ehigh
decls.why: The error ceiling: `(log 2 · r / 8π) · 2^(r/2) · (1 + 2^(−1/2))^(n)`.

decls.name: StmtSchoenfeldWindow
decls.why: Schoenfeld on the window, as a statement: each of the `n+1` values the stencil reads obeys the RH bound at `x = 2^(r−k)`, where `√x = 2^((r−k)/2)` and `log x = (r−k)·log 2`. This is the hypothesis Schoenfeld's theorem would discharge; it is not discharged here.

decls.name: window_term_le
decls.why: Each windowed Schoenfeld bound is at most the top-of-window bound times `2^(−k/2)`: `(r−k) ≤ r` handles the linear factor and `rpow_add` splits the power. Needs `0 ≤ r − k` inside the window, supplied by `hr`.

decls.name: error_bound
decls.why: The error bound. Triangle inequality, the per-term comparison, and the binomial theorem `Σ C(n,k) t^k = (1+t)^n` at `t = 2^(−1/2)`.
needs: hS : StmtSchoenfeldWindow f L r n
decls.proves: |stencilR n (fun x => f x - L x) r| ≤ Ehigh r n

decls.name: Mlow
decls.why: The main-term floor `0.5 · 2^(r−d−1) · (log 2)^d / r`. O67's step 3.

decls.name: nonvanishing_of
decls.why: The arrow. If Schoenfeld holds on the window (`hS`), the smooth main term clears its floor (`hM` — stage 2's target), and the floor beats the error ceiling (`hgap` — O67's `r ≥ R(d)` table), then the depth-`(d+1)` stencil of the counting function does not vanish.
needs: hM : Mlow r d ≤ |stencilR (d + 1) L r|
hgap : Ehigh r (d + 1) < Mlow r d

decls.name: tableFrom_ne_zero_of
decls.why: Onto the integer table. If the integer row is the backward difference of a counting function `f` across the window a cell reads (cast to ℝ), then the cell's vanishing is the depth-`(d+1)` stencil of `f` vanishing — so the arrow above forbids it. The cast bridge is `Zeros.tableFrom_eq_stencil` plus `push_cast`.
needs: hrow : ∀ k ∈ range (d + 2), ((N (r - k) : ℤ) : ℝ) = bdiffZ f (r - k)
hM : Mlow r d ≤ |stencilR (d + 1) L r|
hgap : Ehigh r (d + 1) < Mlow r d

header: Nyquist — why an entire family of integer-base approaches must fail, rather than merely happening to.

decls.name: sample
decls.why: The rungs of a `b`-adic ladder, in `log x`: sampling at `x = b^r` puts the samples at `r * log b`.

decls.name: Aliases
decls.why: Indistinguishable frequencies. `γ` and `γ'` alias on the `b`-adic ladder when their modes agree at every rung. No measurement on the ladder can separate them, because the ladder never evaluates anything else.

decls.name: aliases_of_offset
decls.why: The aliasing offset. Shifting a frequency by `2πk / log b` changes nothing the ladder can see.
decls.proves: Aliases b γ (γ - 2 * π * k / Real.log b)

decls.name: nyquist
decls.why: The Nyquist frequency of a `b`-adic ladder: the highest frequency the rungs can carry without ambiguity.

decls.name: nyquist_no_go
decls.why: THE NO-GO. Past the Nyquist frequency there is always a frequency of strictly smaller modulus that the ladder cannot distinguish from `γ`. So `γ` is not identifiable from `b`-adic samples — not because the measurement is noisy, but because a different answer fits the same data exactly.

decls.name: base_bound_of_resolvable
decls.why: Entry 26's inequality, as the contrapositive. If no smaller-modulus frequency aliases with `γ` — that is, if `γ` really is identifiable from the ladder — then the base is bounded: `b ≤ exp(π/γ)`. For `γ₁` this is the recorded `1.2489`.
needs: hres : ∀ γ', |γ'| < |γ| → ¬ Aliases b γ γ'

decls.name: base_two_past_nyquist
decls.why: Base 2 is past its own Nyquist frequency at every `γ ≥ 14`, and `γ₁ = 14.134…` is such a `γ`. So by `nyquist_no_go`, no dyadic ladder identifies it.

decls.name: base_two_fails_by_three
decls.why: Entry 26's "fails by a factor of three", proved. Three times base 2's Nyquist frequency still does not reach 14, so `γ₁` sits past it with a factor to spare.

header: NyquistPeak — the difference filter's gain at frequency `γ` is stationary, and maximal, exactly at the Nyquist boundary `b* = exp(π/γ)`.

decls.name: gain
decls.why: The gain of the depth-`d` difference filter, as a function of phase. `θ = γ · log b` is the phase one rung of a `b`-ladder advances a mode of frequency `γ`. The definition is written in the prereg's own form; that it is `Chain.Sym`'s modulus is proved, not assumed — see `gain_eq_norm_sym_pow`.

decls.name: sym_on_imaginary_axis
decls.why: The symbol on the imaginary axis is `1 − e^(−iθ)` with `θ = γ log b`.
decls.proves: Chain.Sym b (γ * Complex.I) = 1 - Complex.exp (((-(γ * Real.log b) : ℝ) : ℂ) * Complex.I)

decls.name: norm_sym_on_imaginary_axis
decls.why: The prereg's formula, derived. `‖Chain.Sym b (γ i)‖ = 2 |sin(θ/2)|` with `θ = γ log b`. `preregs/dense_boundary_scan_v1_20260827.md` line 44 writes it `|1 − e^{iθ}|`; this is that modulus, computed from the tree's own symbol rather than restated as a definition.

decls.name: gain_eq_norm_sym_pow
decls.why: The depth-`d` gain is the symbol's modulus to the `d`. This is the link that makes everything below a statement about the object the tree already has.
decls.proves: gain d (γ * Real.log b) = ‖Chain.Sym b (γ * Complex.I)‖ ^ d

decls.name: gain_pi
decls.why: The gain at phase `π` is `2^d` — the ceiling of the band.

decls.name: gain_zero_phase
decls.why: The gain at phase `0` is `0` at every positive depth: the smooth term, having `γ = 0`, is annihilated outright. `Chain.C2_floor_attained` is the critical-line counterpart. This is also the witness that `π` is a strict maximum rather than a plateau.

decls.name: gain_hasDerivAt_pi
decls.why: HALF ONE — the derivative vanishes at `θ = π`. `2|sin(θ/2)|` is smooth on a neighbourhood of `π` (the absolute value is inert there, since `sin` is non-negative on `(0, π)`), and its derivative carries a factor `cos(π/2) = 0`.

decls.name: deriv_gain_pi
decls.why: The same, in `deriv` form.

decls.name: gain_le_gain_pi
decls.why: HALF TWO — `π` is a maximum. Global, not merely local: no phase anywhere reaches a larger gain.
decls.proves: gain d θ ≤ gain d Real.pi

decls.name: gain_lt_gain_pi
decls.why: The maximum is STRICT. At every phase off the peak the gain is strictly smaller, so the stationary point of `gain_hasDerivAt_pi` cannot be a minimum or an inflection. `d ≠ 0` is load-bearing and not a vacuity guard: at `d = 0` the statement is false, since `gain 0` is constant.
decls.proves: gain d θ < gain d Real.pi

decls.name: depth_zero_vacuous
decls.why: The degeneracy the depth hypothesis closes. At `d = 0` the gain is the constant `1`, so `gain_hasDerivAt_pi` — which is true at every depth — says nothing there: every phase is stationary and every phase is a maximum. `#guard_msgs` cannot catch that; a vacuous theorem has an ordinary axiom list. Same shape as `Chain.period_vacuous_at_one`.

decls.name: stationary_maximum
decls.why: § 5.1 in phase coordinates, as one object. Stationary at `π`, and a strict global maximum there.
decls.proves: HasDerivAt (gain d) 0 Real.pi ∧ (∀ θ : ℝ, gain d θ ≤ gain d Real.pi) ∧ (∀ θ : ℝ, |Real.sin (θ / 2)| ≠ 1 → gain d θ < gain d Real.pi)

decls.name: boundaryBase
decls.why: The Nyquist boundary base at frequency `γ`. `Nyquist.nyquist` maps it back to `γ`; see `nyquist_boundaryBase`.

decls.name: boundaryBase_pos
decls.why: The boundary base is positive.

decls.name: one_lt_boundaryBase
decls.why: At a positive frequency the boundary base exceeds `1`, so it lies in the range `Nyquist.base_bound_of_resolvable` speaks about.

decls.name: phase_at_boundaryBase
decls.why: The boundary base puts the phase exactly at `π`. `γ ≠ 0` is load-bearing and its failure makes the statement false, not vacuous: at `γ = 0` Lean's `π/0` is `0`, so `boundaryBase 0 = 1` and the phase is `0`, where `gain_zero_phase` says the gain vanishes.

decls.name: nyquist_boundaryBase
decls.why: `b*` is exactly the base whose Nyquist frequency is `γ`. This is the weld to `lean/Nyquist.lean`: `Nyquist.base_bound_of_resolvable` caps a base that resolves `γ` at `exp(π/γ)`, and that cap is this base.

decls.name: norm_sym_pow_at_boundaryBase
decls.why: The gain at `b*` is the ceiling `2^d`, and it is the symbol's own modulus that reaches it.

decls.name: gain_stationary_in_base
decls.why: HALF ONE, in the scanned coordinate. Sweeping the base through `b*` at fixed frequency `γ`, the `γ` gain has slope exactly zero. This is the statement the dense boundary scan's `no_step` was predicted from: the ingredient does not step at `b*` because it does not even tilt there.
decls.proves: HasDerivAt (fun b : ℝ => gain d (γ * Real.log b)) 0 (boundaryBase γ)

decls.name: gain_continuousAt_boundaryBase
decls.why: Not a discontinuity. Differentiability at `b*` gives continuity there, which is the negative half of the prereg's claim.
decls.proves: ContinuousAt (fun b : ℝ => gain d (γ * Real.log b)) (boundaryBase γ)

decls.name: gain_le_at_boundaryBase
decls.why: HALF TWO, in the scanned coordinate. No base anywhere gives a larger `γ` gain than `b*` does.
decls.proves: gain d (γ * Real.log b) ≤ gain d (γ * Real.log (boundaryBase γ))

decls.name: boundary_is_smooth_stationary_maximum
decls.why: § 5.1, as the prereg states it. For a positive frequency `γ` and a positive depth `d`: `b* = exp(π/γ)` is the base whose Nyquist frequency is `γ`; the `γ` gain is differentiable there with derivative zero; and it is a global maximum over all bases. So `b*` is a smooth stationary maximum of the `γ` response, and nothing in the gain steps across it.
decls.proves: Nyquist.nyquist (boundaryBase γ) = γ ∧ HasDerivAt (fun b : ℝ => gain d (γ * Real.log b)) 0 (boundaryBase γ) ∧ (∀ b : ℝ, gain d (γ * Real.log b) ≤ gain d (γ * Real.log (boundaryBase γ))) ∧ (∀ b : ℝ, |Real.sin (γ * Real.log b / 2)| ≠ 1 → gain d (γ * Real.log b) < gain d (γ * Real.log (boundaryBase γ))) ∧ gain d (γ * Real.log (boundaryBase γ)) = 2 ^ d

header: PairIdentity — the complementary pair, and why base two is singular. Encodes statement **I1** of `papers/Euler-Factor-Chain.md` § I ("The complementary pair"):

decls.name: backward_difference_pow
decls.why: The same step inside ℤ, where the table lives: `(1 − b⁻¹)·b^(r) = (b−1)·b^(r−1)`. One backward difference of a geometric row multiplies it by `b − 1` and drops the exponent by one.

decls.name: tableFrom_of_geometric
decls.why: The collapse. If the row steps by `b` across the window a cell reads, then `d` backward differences leave `(b−1)^d` times the bottom entry of that window. Iterating `backward_difference_pow`; the whole index difficulty is that each difference moves the window's bottom down by one.
needs: hG : ∀ k : ℕ, k < d → G (r - k) = b * G (r - k - 1)
decls.proves: tableFrom G r d = (b - 1) ^ d * G (r - d)

decls.name: tableFrom_add_window
decls.why: Linearity, localised. If two rows partition a third across the window a cell reads, the two tables sum to the third table at that cell. `Construction.tableFrom_add` gives that the table of a sum is the sum of tables; `Construction.zero_determined_by_row` gives that agreement on the window is all a cell can see.
needs: h : ∀ k : ℕ, k ≤ d → P (r - k) + C (r - k) = T (r - k)
decls.proves: tableFrom P r d + tableFrom C r d = tableFrom T r d

decls.name: pair_identity
decls.why: I1, the pair identity. Let `P` and `C` be any two rows that partition each rung: at rung `r − k` the two counts sum to `(b−1)·b^(r−k−1)`, the number of integers the rung holds. Then at every cell the differenced arms sum to
needs: hpair : ∀ k : ℕ, k ≤ d → P (r - k) + C (r - k) = (b - 1) * b ^ (e + (d - k))
decls.proves: tableFrom P r d + tableFrom C r d = (b - 1) ^ (d + 1) * b ^ e

decls.name: composite_of_prime_zero
decls.why: I5, the pole. Where the prime arm vanishes the composite arm carries the whole total — it has nowhere else to go. This is the identity read at a zero, and it is the only sense in which a zero says anything about the composite side.
needs: hpair : ∀ k : ℕ, k ≤ d → P (r - k) + C (r - k) = (b - 1) * b ^ (e + (d - k))
decls.proves: tableFrom C r d = (b - 1) ^ (d + 1) * b ^ e

decls.name: coeff_eq_one_iff_base_two
decls.why: The corollary. For integer `b ≥ 2`, the coefficient `(b−1)^(d+1)` is `1` exactly when `b = 2`. Every other base carries a factor strictly greater than one, at every depth.

decls.name: total_eq_pow_iff_base_two
decls.why: The corollary, in the identity's own terms. The cell total is a bare power of the base — no `(b−1)` factor anywhere — exactly in base two. So base two is the only grid on which a vanished prime arm leaves the composite arm sitting on a power of the base itself.

decls.name: base_three_carries_factor
decls.why: Base three does carry the factor: the total at `(r,d)` is `2^(d+1)·3^(r−1−d)`, never a bare power of three.

decls.name: base_four_carries_factor
decls.why: Base four likewise: `3^(d+1)·4^(r−1−d)`.

decls.name: exponent_const_on_diagonal
decls.why: Along a diagonal the pair identity's exponent is fixed. `hdiag` is `r − d` constant; `h₁` and `h₂` are the index convention, which pins `e = r − 1 − d`.

decls.name: total_const_on_diagonal
decls.why: The diagonal is the trend's own level set, and only at `b = 2`. Fix a diagonal — equivalently, fix `e` — and ask whether the cell total is the same at every depth along it. It is, exactly in base two.

decls.name: zero_cells
decls.why: The four exact zeros of the dyadic prime table, `(r, d)`, `r ≤ 62`, `d ≤ 61`. `results/O16_run2.log`; same list as `Zeros.measured_zeros` and `Construction.measured_zeros`.

decls.name: measured_composite_at_zeros
decls.why: The composite arm at those four cells, read from `papers/The-Four-Zeros.md` § E2: "At the four zeros the composite arm therefore carries the whole term: `1, 4, 16, 8192`."

decls.name: measured_composite_matches_pair_identity
decls.why: The falsifier. Evaluating `(b−1)^(d+1)·b^(r−1−d)` at `b = 2` and the four measured zero cells reproduces the measured composite arm exactly. The formula is derived above from the partition alone; the four values were measured. They agree.

decls.name: composite_at_zero_20_6
decls.why: The deep zero, stated through the identity rather than through arithmetic. Given that the prime arm vanishes at `(20,6)` — which is measured, not proved — the partition forces the composite arm to be `8192`, which is what § E2 records.

header: Propagation — the recurrence as transport: the light cone, and the propagator. `papers/Depth-as-Time.md` reads depth as time. Take that literally: with `d` as time and `r` as space, the recurrence

decls.name: pasc
decls.why: Binomial coefficients by the Pascal recurrence, ℤ-valued. Core has no `Nat.choose`; defining it this way makes Pascal's identity definitional.

decls.name: pasc_zero
decls.why: The left edge of the triangle is all ones.

decls.name: pasc_succ
decls.why: Pascal's identity — definitional, because `pasc` is defined by it.
decls.proves: pasc (n + 1) (k + 1) = pasc n k + pasc n (k + 1)

decls.name: pasc_eq_zero
decls.why: Above the diagonal the binomial vanishes.

decls.name: pasc_pos
decls.why: On and below the diagonal it is positive — this is what "no lacunae" rests on: the propagator never vanishes inside its cone.

decls.name: deltaRow
decls.why: A unit disturbance at rung `s`: the delta row.

decls.name: outside_cone_zero
decls.why: Outside the forward cone, nothing. A source at `s` does not reach a cell whose window `[r−d, r]` misses `s` — the range of influence is bounded by speed 1. Downstream (`r < s`) and past the cone's left edge (`s < r−d`) the cell is zero.
needs: h : r < s ∨ s < r - (d : ℤ)

decls.name: propagator
decls.why: Inside the cone, the propagator. At offset `k ≤ d` from the source the cell is exactly `(−1)^k · C(d,k)`: the Green's function of the evolution is the alternating binomial row — the stencil, read as a propagator.
decls.proves: tableFrom (deltaRow s) (s + (k : ℤ)) d = (-1) ^ k * pasc d k

decls.name: neg_one_pow
decls.why: `(−1)^m` is `1` or `−1`. Stated here because core carries no pow lemmas.

decls.name: cone_filled
decls.why: No lacunae. Strictly inside the forward cone the disturbance is felt at EVERY cell — the propagator never vanishes there. Discrete 1+1 transport fills its cone, where the 3+1 wave equation would leave the interior silent.

decls.name: flux_form
decls.why: The flux form. The recurrence rearranged as a conservation step: what the cell holds at time `d+1` plus what flowed left is what it held at `d`. Definitional — recorded so the transport reading has its conservation law stated. The interval form (a sum at time `d+1` telescoping to boundary terms) is `Isogeny.telescope`, on the Mathlib side.
decls.proves: tableFrom N r (d + 1) + tableFrom N (r - 1) d = tableFrom N r d

header: RelativeGate — the census gate, stated without assuming an error shape. WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. `Nonvanishing.lean` states the census gate in the RH shape: `StmtSchoenfeldWindow` carries `√x·log x/(8π)` per value, and `Ehigh` accumulates it into `2^(r/2)·(1+2^(−1/2))^n`. Every downstream tolerance study (O68, entry 118) then swept the family `C·√x·(log x)^k` — every row RH-strength. Whether the gate NEEDS that shape was never asked, and the answer was assumed rather than derived.

decls.name: StmtRelErrWindow
decls.why: Relative error on the window. Each of the `n+1` values the stencil reads sits within `ρ` times its own scale `2^m`. No functional form is assumed — this is the weakest hypothesis the gate can consume.

decls.name: EhighRel
decls.why: The accumulated ceiling under a relative-error hypothesis: `ρ·2^r·(3/2)^n`. The per-value scale halves down the window, so the binomial sum contributes `Σ C(n,k) 2^(−k) = (3/2)^n` — the exact analogue of `Ehigh`'s `(1+2^(−1/2))^n`, with `2^(−1/2)` replaced by `2^(−1)`.

decls.name: relWindow_term_le
decls.why: Each windowed relative bound is the top-of-window scale times `2^(−k)`.

decls.name: relError_bound
decls.why: The error bound, shape-free. Triangle inequality, the per-term scale, and the binomial theorem at `t = 1/2`.
needs: hS : StmtRelErrWindow f L r n ρ
decls.proves: |stencilR n (fun x => f x - L x) r| ≤ EhighRel r n ρ

decls.name: relGate_iff
decls.why: THE GATE, REDUCED. The census condition against a relative-error ceiling is a bound on `ρ` alone — the scale `2^r` appears on both sides and cancels. What survives is
decls.proves: EhighRel r (d + 1) ρ < Mlow r d ↔ ρ < Real.log 2 ^ d / (2 * r * 3 ^ (d + 1))

decls.name: relGate_eps
decls.why: The threshold as a single constant divided by `log x`: with `log x = r·log 2`, the gate reads `ρ < ε_d / log x` where `ε_d = 0.5·(log 2/3)^(d+1)`. The constant falls by `3/log 2 ≈ 4.33` per unit of depth.

decls.name: nonvanishing_of_relErr
decls.why: The arrow, with no assumption on the error's shape.
needs: hS : StmtRelErrWindow f L r (d + 1) ρ
hM : Mlow r d ≤ |stencilR (d + 1) L r|
hgap : EhighRel r (d + 1) ρ < Mlow r d

decls.name: tableFrom_ne_zero_of_relErr
decls.why: Onto the integer table, shape-free. Mirrors `Nonvanishing.tableFrom_ne_zero_of` with the relative-error hypothesis in place of the Schoenfeld one.
needs: hrow : ∀ k ∈ range (d + 2), ((N (r - k) : ℤ) : ℝ) = bdiffZ f (r - k)
hS : StmtRelErrWindow f L r (d + 1) ρ
hM : Mlow r d ≤ |stencilR (d + 1) L r|
hgap : EhighRel r (d + 1) ρ < Mlow r d

decls.name: schoenfeldWindow_relErr
decls.why: The weld to the RH layer. `Nonvanishing.StmtSchoenfeldWindow` is an instance of the shape-free hypothesis. The relative error is worst at the window BOTTOM — `√x/x = 2^(−m/2)` grows as `m` falls — so the witness is `ρ = (log 2·r/(8π))·2^(−(r−n)/2)`, not the top-of-window value. Both factors are then bounded termwise: `r−k ≤ r` for the linear one, `k ≤ n` for the exponential one.
needs: hS : Nonvanishing.StmtSchoenfeldWindow f L r n
decls.proves: StmtRelErrWindow f L r n ((Real.log 2 * r / (8 * Real.pi)) * (2 : ℝ) ^ (-((r : ℝ) - n) / 2))

decls.name: powerSaving_relErr
decls.why: The power-saving instance. A bound `|f − L| ≤ A·x^θ` at `x = 2^m` gives relative error `A·2^(m(θ−1))`, worst at the window bottom when `θ ≤ 1`. So the witness is `ρ = A·2^((r−n)(θ−1))`, and the gate becomes a statement about the exponent `θ` alone.
decls.proves: StmtRelErrWindow f L r n (A * (2 : ℝ) ^ (((r : ℝ) - n) * (θ - 1)))

header: RelativeLi — the relative-error gate with its main term discharged. `RelativeGate.tableFrom_ne_zero_of_relErr` makes a cell nonzero from a relative error on a window of rows, a floor `hM` under the main term's stencil, and the gap. `Expansion.hD_of_window` with `MainTerm.stencilR_ge_of` proves that floor for a smooth interpolant `G` of `li` along the doublings (`G' = 2^x/x`). Nothing composed them: the Schoenfeld-shaped gate had its composition (`Expansion.tableFrom_ne_zero_of_li`), the shape-free gate did not. Thi…

decls.name: tableFrom_ne_zero_of_relErr_li
decls.why: The shape-free gate on the table, main term discharged.
needs: hG' : ∀ x ∈ Ioi ((1 : ℝ) / 2), HasDerivAt G (Expansion.f2x x) x
hrow : ∀ k ∈ range (d + 2), ((N (r - k) : ℤ) : ℝ) = Nonvanishing.bdiffZ f (r - k)
hS : RelativeGate.StmtRelErrWindow f (fun k : ℤ => G k) r (d + 1) ρ
hgap : RelativeGate.EhighRel r (d + 1) ρ < Nonvanishing.Mlow r d

decls.name: tableFrom_ne_zero_of_relErr_li'
decls.why: The same with the gap reduced to a bound on `ρ` alone.
needs: hG' : ∀ x ∈ Ioi ((1 : ℝ) / 2), HasDerivAt G (Expansion.f2x x) x
hrow : ∀ k ∈ range (d + 2), ((N (r - k) : ℤ) : ℝ) = Nonvanishing.bdiffZ f (r - k)
hS : RelativeGate.StmtRelErrWindow f (fun k : ℤ => G k) r (d + 1) ρ

decls.name: tableFrom_ne_zero_of_powerSaving
decls.why: From a power bound on the rows. `|f(m) − G(m)| ≤ A·(2^m)^θ` on the window with `θ ≤ 1`, and `A·2^((r−d−1)(θ−1))` under the gate's threshold.
needs: hG' : ∀ x ∈ Ioi ((1 : ℝ) / 2), HasDerivAt G (Expansion.f2x x) x
hrow : ∀ k ∈ range (d + 2), ((N (r - k) : ℤ) : ℝ) = Nonvanishing.bdiffZ f (r - k)

header: RouteCell — block E9 of `lean_stage3/design/joints.md`, the table tree's half. The gate (`Interpolant.tableFrom_ne_zero_of_relErr_liRow`) at depth six, on the statement the other tree's explicit-formula route proves under RH.

decls.name: cell_ne_zero_of_route
needs: hrow : ∀ k ∈ Finset.range (6 + 2), ((N (r - k) : ℤ) : ℝ) = Nonvanishing.bdiffZ f (r - k)
hroute : ∃ ρ : ℝ, RelativeGate.StmtRelErrWindow f (fun m : ℤ => 2 / Real.log 2 + ∫ t in (1 : ℝ)..(m : ℝ), Real.exp (Real.log 2 * t) / t) r (6 + 1) ρ ∧ ρ < Real.log 2 ^ 6 / (2 * r * 3 ^ (6 + 1))

header: Schoenfeld — stage 3's interface: the literature sentence, verbatim. `Expansion.tableFrom_ne_zero_of_li` carries the conditional arrow with `hS` stated window-wise, in bench shape: per-`k` bounds with the power already translated to `2^((r−k)/2)`. Nobody can check that against Schoenfeld 1976 by eye. This module moves the unproven surface to the exact cited sentence:

decls.name: StmtSchoenfeld
decls.why: Schoenfeld 1976, Corollary 1, verbatim shape: for all `x ≥ 2657`, `|π(x) − li(x)| ≤ √x · log x / (8π)`. RH-conditional in the literature; here a named hypothesis over abstract `pi li : ℝ → ℝ`.

decls.name: window_of_global
decls.why: The bridge: the global sentence implies the bench-shaped window hypothesis whenever the window bottom clears `12`, since `2^12 = 4096 ≥ 2657`. The translation is `√(2^y) = 2^(y/2)` and `log(2^y) = y·log 2`.
needs: hf : ∀ m : ℤ, f m = pi ((2 : ℝ) ^ (m : ℝ))
hL : ∀ m : ℤ, L m = li ((2 : ℝ) ^ (m : ℝ))

decls.name: tableFrom_ne_zero_of_schoenfeld
decls.why: The arrow, with the literature sentence as its one analytic input. Identical to `Expansion.tableFrom_ne_zero_of_li` except that `hS` is replaced by `StmtSchoenfeld` — Schoenfeld's published inequality character for character — plus the compatibility of `f` and `G` with `pi` and `li` at the points `2^m`, and the window bottom raised to `12 ≤ r − (d+1)` so every window point clears Schoenfeld's floor `x ≥ 2657`.
needs: hG' : ∀ x ∈ Ioi ((1 : ℝ) / 2), HasDerivAt G (Expansion.f2x x) x
hf : ∀ m : ℤ, f m = pi ((2 : ℝ) ^ (m : ℝ))
hli : ∀ m : ℤ, G (m : ℝ) = li ((2 : ℝ) ^ (m : ℝ))
hrow : ∀ k ∈ range (d + 2), ((N (r - k) : ℤ) : ℝ) = Nonvanishing.bdiffZ f (r - k)
hgap : Nonvanishing.Ehigh r (d + 1) < Nonvanishing.Mlow r d

header: SeedPerturbation — changing the seed convention cannot reach a deep cell. THE QUESTION. The dyadic tables in `imported/lattice_mapper/` are built on a seed convention: the primes 2 and 3 are treated as lattice rather than counted as primes. That is a choice. If a different choice moved the zeros, the zeros would be artefacts of bookkeeping. So: which cells can a change of convention reach?

decls.name: tableFrom_zero
decls.why: The zero row builds the zero table.

decls.name: tableFrom_sub
decls.why: Linearity, in the form the convention change needs. Replacing the depth-0 row `N` by `N − e` subtracts `tableFrom e` from every cell of the table, at every depth.
decls.proves: tableFrom (fun x => N x - e x) r d = tableFrom N r d - tableFrom e r d

decls.name: tableFrom_eq_zero_of_vanishing_above
decls.why: The excess table vanishes past the excess. If `e` is zero on every rung strictly above `R`, then every cell whose window bottom `r − d` clears `R` reads only zeros, so the cell is zero.
needs: he : ∀ s : ℤ, R < s → e s = 0

decls.name: cell_eq_of_seed_perturbation
decls.why: The claim. Changing the seed convention replaces the depth-0 row `N` by `N − e`. If `e` vanishes on every rung strictly above `R`, then every cell at `(r,d)` with `r − d > R` is IDENTICAL under both conventions.
needs: he : ∀ s : ℤ, R < s → e s = 0
decls.proves: tableFrom (fun x => N x - e x) r d = tableFrom N r d

decls.name: zero_stable_of_seed_perturbation
decls.why: The corollary. A zero at `(r,d)` with `r − d > R` is a zero under both conventions. The seed convention cannot have put it there and cannot take it away.
needs: he : ∀ s : ℤ, R < s → e s = 0
decls.proves: tableFrom (fun x => N x - e x) r d = 0

decls.name: zero_iff_of_seed_perturbation
decls.why: The same statement as an equivalence, which is the honest form: past the excess, the two conventions have the same zero set. Neither direction is a weaker claim than the other.
needs: he : ∀ s : ℤ, R < s → e s = 0
decls.proves: tableFrom (fun x => N x - e x) r d = 0 ↔ tableFrom N r d = 0

decls.name: tableFrom_at_boundary
decls.why: The boundary cell, exactly. When the window bottom sits on `R` itself, `d` backward differences leave `(−1)^d · e R` — the whole excess, signed. Every higher entry of the window is already zero, so the bottom entry is all there is.
needs: he : ∀ s : ℤ, R < s → e s = 0
decls.proves: tableFrom e r d = (-1) ^ d * e R

decls.name: boundary_can_move
decls.why: `r − d > R` cannot be relaxed to `r − d ≥ R`. Take `R` to be the largest rung where `e` is non-zero, which is what `R_e` means. Then every cell with `r − d = R` moves, by exactly `±e R`. The strict inequality is not slack in the proof; it is the boundary.
needs: he : ∀ s : ℤ, R < s → e s = 0

decls.name: cell_ne_at_boundary
decls.why: The same fact said about the two conventions rather than about `e`: at the boundary the cell genuinely differs.
needs: he : ∀ s : ℤ, R < s → e s = 0
decls.proves: tableFrom (fun x => N x - e x) r d ≠ tableFrom N r d

decls.name: zero_cells
decls.why: The four exact zeros of the dyadic prime table, `(r, d)`. Same list as `Zeros.measured_zeros`, `Construction.measured_zeros`, `PairIdentity.zero_cells`; re-read here from `imported/lattice_mapper/32bit/dyadic_difference_table_32.csv`.

decls.name: zero_window_bottoms
decls.why: The window bottoms `r − d` of the four zeros.

decls.name: window_bottoms_correct
decls.why: The window bottoms `r − d` of the four zeros are `1, 3, 5, 14`, computed rather than transcribed.

decls.name: protected_at_R_two
decls.why: Which zeros the theorem protects when 2 and 3 are the excluded primes. `R_e = 2`, so `(2,1)` is unprotected and the other three are fixed. This is the prediction, stated before looking at any perturbed table.
decls.proves: zero_cells.map (fun c => decide (2 < (c.1 : ℤ) - (c.2 : ℤ))) = [false, true, true, true]

decls.name: protected_at_R_three
decls.why: And when the excess reaches rung 3 — which `silence46` does, since 6 sits in `(4,8]`. Now `(4,1)` falls to the boundary as well.
decls.proves: zero_cells.map (fun c => decide (3 < (c.1 : ℤ) - (c.2 : ℤ))) = [false, false, true, true]

decls.name: silence46_excess
decls.why: The measured excess for `silence46`: one silenced number in rung 2, one in rung 3, nothing above.

decls.name: silence46_vanishes_above_three
decls.why: The `silence46` excess is confined to rungs 2 and 3 — the hypothesis `cell_eq_of_seed_perturbation` needs, at `R_e = 3`.

decls.name: silence46_alive_at_three
decls.why: And rung 3 genuinely carries excess, so `boundary_can_move` has its `e R ≠ 0`.

decls.name: measured_composite
decls.why: Cells `(4,1)`, `(8,3)`, `(20,6)` of `dyadic_composite_difference_table_32.csv`.

decls.name: measured_composite_silence46
decls.why: The same three cells of `dyadic_composite_difference_table_32_silence46.csv`.

decls.name: measured_silence46_matches_shift
decls.why: The falsifier. Subtracting `tableFrom silence46_excess` from the three measured base cells reproduces the three measured silenced cells exactly — including the one that MOVED. `(4,1)` sits at `r − d = 3 = R_e`, and the shift `tableFrom e 4 1 = −1` carries 4 to 5, which is what the file says. `(8,3)` and `(20,6)` clear `R_e` and do not move.
decls.proves: [4 - tableFrom silence46_excess 4 1, 16 - tableFrom silence46_excess 8 3, 8192 - tableFrom silence46_excess 20 6] = measured_composite_silence46

decls.name: silence46_deep_cells_fixed
decls.why: The two deep cells are protected by the theorem, not by arithmetic luck: `8 − 3 = 5 > 3` and `20 − 6 = 14 > 3`, so `cell_eq_of_seed_perturbation` applies and no computation is needed.
decls.proves: tableFrom (fun x => N x - silence46_excess x) 8 3 = tableFrom N 8 3 ∧ tableFrom (fun x => N x - silence46_excess x) 20 6 = tableFrom N 20 6

decls.name: silence46_cell_4_1_moves
decls.why: And `(4,1)` is not protected, for the reason the theorem gives rather than by inspection: `4 − 1 = 3 = R_e`, so `boundary_can_move` fires.
decls.proves: tableFrom (fun x => N x - silence46_excess x) 4 1 ≠ tableFrom N 4 1

decls.name: emptied_excess
decls.why: The measured excess for the emptied variant: rung 1 loses one, rung 2 loses two, nothing above.

decls.name: emptied_vanishes_above_two
decls.why: The emptied variant's excess is confined to rungs 1 and 2 — `R_e = 2`, the same profile as excluding the primes 2 and 3.

decls.name: measured_composite_four
decls.why: Cells `(2,1)`, `(4,1)`, `(8,3)`, `(20,6)` of `dyadic_composite_difference_table_32.csv`.

decls.name: measured_emptied_four
decls.why: The same four cells of `dyadic_composite_extended_emptied_32.csv`.

decls.name: measured_emptied_matches_shift
decls.why: The second falsifier, at `R_e = 2`. The three cells the theorem protects are unmoved in the file, and the one it does not protect — `(2,1)`, window bottom `1` — moved from 1 to 0, by exactly the predicted shift `tableFrom e 2 1 = e 2 − e 1 = 1`.
decls.proves: [1 - tableFrom emptied_excess 2 1, 4 - tableFrom emptied_excess 4 1, 16 - tableFrom emptied_excess 8 3, 8192 - tableFrom emptied_excess 20 6] = measured_emptied_four

decls.name: emptied_protected_cells_fixed
decls.why: The three protected cells, again by theorem rather than by computation: `4 − 1 = 3 > 2`, `8 − 3 = 5 > 2`, `20 − 6 = 14 > 2`.
decls.proves: tableFrom (fun x => N x - emptied_excess x) 4 1 = tableFrom N 4 1 ∧ tableFrom (fun x => N x - emptied_excess x) 8 3 = tableFrom N 8 3 ∧ tableFrom (fun x => N x - emptied_excess x) 20 6 = tableFrom N 20 6

header: Superposition — the missing licence for building the residual from the zeros. `Chain.A4_of_A1` gives the depth-N gain for a SINGLE mode. Every use of it on the bench applies it to a SUM over zeta zeros (O34, O35). Nothing so far permits that step. This file supplies it, and nothing else.

decls.name: modeSum
decls.why: A finite superposition of ladder modes.

decls.name: bdiff_sum
decls.why: `bdiff` distributes over a finite sum.
decls.proves: bdiff (fun r => ∑ i ∈ s, f i r) = fun r => ∑ i ∈ s, bdiff (f i) r

decls.name: A4_sum_of_A1
decls.why: The licence. If A1 holds for every mode in the family, then `N` differences act on the superposition by acting on each mode separately. This is what permits applying the depth gain to a sum over zeros.
needs: hA1 : ∀ i ∈ s, StmtA1 b (ρ i)
decls.proves: ∀ (N : ℕ) (r : ℂ), (bdiff^[N]) (modeSum b ρ c s) r = ∑ i ∈ s, c i * (Sym b (ρ i)) ^ N * mode b (ρ i) r

decls.name: depth_reweights_each_mode
decls.why: Corollary — the falsifiable form. Every mode is scaled by its own gain, so the depth-`N` superposition is the depth-0 one with each term reweighted by `(Sym b ρᵢ)^N`. The measured fractions in O34 test this model; they are not inputs to it.
needs: hA1 : ∀ i ∈ s, StmtA1 b (ρ i)
decls.proves: (bdiff^[N]) (modeSum b ρ c s) r = modeSum b ρ (fun i => c i * (Sym b (ρ i)) ^ N) s r

decls.name: tableFrom_eq_modeSum_reweighted
decls.why: The table is a superposition, reweighted by depth. An integer row agreeing at every integer with a finite superposition of ladder modes: its cell at `(r,d)` is that superposition with each mode carrying its own `(Sym b ρᵢ)^d`.
needs: hA1 : ∀ i ∈ s, StmtA1 b (ρ i)
hag : ∀ n : ℤ, ((N n : ℤ) : ℂ) = modeSum b ρ c s (n : ℂ)
decls.proves: ((Construction.tableFrom N r d : ℤ) : ℂ) = modeSum b ρ (fun i => c i * (Sym b (ρ i)) ^ d) s (r : ℂ)

header: TransferOp — bdiff named as the operator it is, in Mathlib's own vocabulary. `papers/Depth-as-Time.md` reads depth as iteration: each mode `x^ρ` is multiplied by `(1 − b^(−ρ))` per step (A2), the operator has a growth factor per mode (A3), and the first Riemann zero is the fastest-growing mode of the difference operator in base 2 (B4). That is transfer-operator vocabulary — `bdiff` is the transfer operator of the ladder shift, the modes are its eigenfunctions, `Sym` its multiplier — and none of it was stated in the…

decls.name: bdiffL
decls.why: `Chain.bdiff`, packaged as a linear endomorphism of the function space. The linearity was consumed all over the tree (`bdiff_smul`, `Superposition.bdiff_sum`) and never stated as a structure.

decls.name: bdiffL_apply
decls.why: The packaging is definitional: applying the endomorphism is applying `bdiff`.

decls.name: mode_ne_zero'
decls.why: A mode never vanishes: `b^(rρ) ≠ 0` for `b ≠ 0`.

decls.name: mode_ne_zero
decls.why: Hence a mode is not the zero function.

decls.name: mode_hasEigenvector
decls.why: The mode is an eigenvector, in Mathlib's sense. `Chain.A1` is the pointwise identity; this is the same fact carried into `Module.End.HasEigenvector`, which is what makes the operator reading a structure rather than a description.

decls.name: sym_hasEigenvalue
decls.why: `Sym b ρ` is in the point spectrum. Every value of the symbol is an eigenvalue of the difference operator.

decls.name: mode_pow
decls.why: Depth is the operator power on the eigenline. `(bdiffL^N) mode = Sym^N • mode` — `Chain.A4` as an operator identity, via Mathlib's `HasEigenvector.pow_apply`.
decls.proves: (bdiffL ^ N) (mode b ρ) = (Sym b ρ) ^ N • mode b ρ

decls.name: eigenvalue_zero_iff_lattice
decls.why: The kernel eigenvalue sits exactly on the pole lattice. The mode is annihilated — eigenvalue 0 — precisely when `ρ ∈ (2πi/log b)·ℤ`, which is `Chain.sym_eq_zero_iff` read as a statement about the operator. This is the lattice `Transform.sym_zero_on_outer_circle` carries to `|z| = 1`.
decls.proves: bdiffL (mode b ρ) = 0 ↔ ∃ k : ℤ, ρ = (k : ℂ) * (2 * Real.pi * I / Real.log b)

header: Transform — block G's geometry: the strip, the annulus, and what closes it. `papers/Euler-Factor-Chain.md` § G is listed as **not formalised** in `lean/BUILD.md`, and most of it is measurement (G2, G4, G5, G7 from O39) or literature (G3 Jentzsch, G9 Hardy, G10 Odlyzko–te Riele). This file takes the part that is geometry.

decls.name: norm_zmap
decls.why: The map. `z = b^(−s)` sends the vertical line `Re s = σ` to the circle `|z| = b^(−σ)`.

decls.name: norm_zmap_critical
decls.why: The critical line lands on the circle of radius `b^(−1/2)`.

decls.name: zmap_shift
decls.why: The deck transformation. `s ↦ s + 1` becomes `z ↦ z / b`. This is the identification that closes the annulus into a torus: `ℂ* / b^ℤ`.

decls.name: zmap_period
decls.why: The other generator. `s ↦ s + 2πi/log b` leaves `z` fixed — that is the pole lattice, and it is why the strip maps to an annulus rather than a plane.
decls.proves: (b : ℂ) ^ (-(s + 2 * Real.pi * I / Real.log b)) = (b : ℂ) ^ (-s)

decls.name: zmap_functional_equation
decls.why: The functional equation, in `z`. `s ↦ 1 − s` becomes `z ↦ b^(−1)/z`, inversion in the circle `|z| = b^(−1/2)` — which is the critical line.

decls.name: annulus_modulus
decls.why: G7's modulus. The annulus between the two radii has conformal modulus `(log b)/4π`. Its ratio is `√b`, so it is half a fundamental domain of `ℂ* / b^ℤ`, whose modulus is `(log b)/2π`.
decls.proves: Real.log (b ^ (-(1:ℝ)/2) / b ^ (-(1:ℝ))) / (2 * Real.pi) = Real.log b / (4 * Real.pi)

decls.name: tau
decls.why: The torus `ℂ*/b^ℤ` has lattice `⟨1, 2πi/log b⟩` in `s`, so its modular parameter is `τ = 2πi/log b`. This is its imaginary part.

decls.name: zmap_period_tau
decls.why: `τ` is exactly the period `zmap_period` uses.

decls.name: tau_pow
decls.why: The power chain. `τ(b^n) = τ(b)/n`. This is why `{2,4,8}` is one family: `τ₄ = τ₂/2` and `τ₈ = τ₂/3`.

decls.name: tau_ratio_of_meet
decls.why: Meeting ladders have rationally related `τ`, and the ratio is the meeting exponents. If `b^n = c^m` then `τ(b)/τ(c) = n/m`. `Zeros.primeFactors_eq_of_meets` records the arithmetic side: ladders meet only inside a prime-power chain.
decls.proves: tau b / tau c = n / m

decls.name: poleLattice
decls.why: The pole lattice alone: integer multiples of the period `τ(b)·i`. The `z`-map is constant on its cosets, which is why the strip becomes an annulus.

decls.name: periodLattice
decls.why: The full period lattice in `s`: generated by `1`, the deck transformation, and `τ(b)·i`, the pole lattice.

decls.name: Torus
decls.why: The torus. `ℂ ⧸ ⟨1, τ(b)·i⟩` — the object `ℂ*/b^ℤ` names.

decls.name: one_mem_periodLattice
decls.why: The deck generator `1` is in the lattice.

decls.name: tauI_mem_periodLattice
decls.why: The period generator `τ(b)·i` is in the lattice.

decls.name: tau_pos
decls.why: `τ(b) > 0` for `b > 1`, which is what makes the second generator nonzero.

decls.name: generators_indep
decls.why: The lattice has rank 2. The two generators are ℝ-linearly independent: one is real, the other purely imaginary and nonzero. This is what separates a torus from a cylinder, and it is the only place `b > 1` is needed.

decls.name: gens
decls.why: The two generators as a family, for the basis construction below.

decls.name: gens_linearIndependent
decls.why: `generators_indep` in the form Mathlib's basis constructor wants.

decls.name: latticeBasis
decls.why: The lattice basis. `⟨1, τ(b)·i⟩` is an ℝ-basis of ℂ, so the subgroup it generates is a rank-2 ℤ-lattice in a 2-dimensional ℝ-space.

decls.name: periodLattice_eq_span
decls.why: The additive closure of the two generators is the ℤ-span of the basis — the bridge from `AddSubgroup.closure` to the `ZLattice` instance that `periodLattice_discrete` consumes.

decls.name: periodLattice_discrete
decls.why: The lattice is discrete. This is what upgrades `ℂ ⧸ periodLattice b` from a quotient by a subgroup to a torus: a rank-2 ℤ-span of an ℝ-basis carries the discrete topology, so the quotient is Hausdorff and the fibres are isolated. The docstring above this section claimed this was left unproved; it is proved here.

decls.name: torus_shift
decls.why: The deck transformation is an identity in the torus.

decls.name: torus_period
decls.why: The period is an identity in the torus.
decls.proves: ((s + (tau b : ℂ) * I : ℂ) : Torus b) = (s : Torus b)

decls.name: zmap_period_zsmul
decls.why: The `z`-map descends past the whole pole lattice, not just one period. `zmap_period` is the `n = 1` case.

decls.name: zmap_shift_modulus
decls.why: The deck transformation scales the modulus by `b^(−n)`. This is the `b^ℤ` in `ℂ*/b^ℤ`: at `b = 2` it identifies `|z| = … 0.5 ~ 1 ~ 2 ~ 4 …`, so every 2:1 annulus is a fundamental domain.

decls.name: inversion_fixes_circle
decls.why: The functional equation is inversion in the critical circle, as a theorem. `z ↦ b^(−1)/z` preserves modulus exactly on `|z| = b^(−1/2)` — the image of the critical line. The geometric reading in `zmap_functional_equation` was a docstring until here.

decls.name: rpow_left_inj
decls.why: For `b > 1` the real power is injective in the exponent.
decls.proves: b ^ x = b ^ y ↔ x = y

decls.name: zmap_ne_zero
decls.why: The image of `s` under the `z`-map is never zero.

decls.name: on_critical_line_iff_norm
decls.why: The critical line is exactly the fixed circle. `Re s = 1/2` iff the image `b^(−s)` lands on `|z| = b^(−1/2)`.

decls.name: on_critical_line_iff_inversion_fixed
decls.why: RH's condition, as a fixed point of the inversion. `Re s = 1/2` iff `b^(−s)` is fixed in modulus by `z ↦ b^(−1)/z`, which `zmap_functional_equation` identifies as `s ↦ 1 − s`.

decls.name: riemannHypothesis_iff_zeros_inversion_fixed
decls.why: The Riemann hypothesis, restated on the torus. Mathlib's `RiemannHypothesis` holds exactly when every nontrivial zero of `ζ` is carried by `z = b^(−s)` to a fixed point of the inversion `z ↦ b^(−1)/z`.
decls.proves: RiemannHypothesis ↔ ∀ (s : ℂ), riemannZeta s = 0 → ¬(∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * (n + 1)) → s ≠ 1 → ‖(b : ℂ) ^ (-(1 : ℂ)) / (b : ℂ) ^ (-s)‖ = ‖(b : ℂ) ^ (-s)‖

decls.name: norm_zmap_zero_line
decls.why: `Re s = 0` lands on the unit circle.

decls.name: strip_is_fundamental_domain
decls.why: The critical strip is one fundamental domain of `ℂ*/b^ℤ`. Its left edge maps to `|z| = 1`, its right edge to `|z| = b^(−1)`, and the two are a single deck step apart — `s ↦ s + 1`, which `zmap_shift` sends to `z ↦ z/b`.

decls.name: zeros_re_lt_one
decls.why: Every zero of ζ has `Re s < 1`, from Mathlib's non-vanishing on the closed half-plane `1 ≤ Re s`.

decls.name: zeros_outside_inner_circle
decls.why: Every zero lies strictly outside the inner circle. `Re s < 1` becomes `|z| > b^(−1)` — the zeros are inside the fundamental annulus, on the far side of the boundary the Euler product owns.

decls.name: zeros_re_pos
decls.why: Every nontrivial zero has `0 < Re s`. The functional equation reflects Mathlib's non-vanishing on `1 ≤ Re s` across to the left edge: at a zero with `Re s ≤ 0` every factor of `riemannZeta_one_sub` is nonzero except the cosine, and the cosine's zeros are exactly the trivial zeros together with `s = 0`, where `ζ(0) = −1/2`.

decls.name: zeros_in_fundamental_annulus
decls.why: Every nontrivial zero lies in the open fundamental annulus. `b^(−1) < |z| < 1` — and `strip_is_fundamental_domain` says that annulus is exactly one fundamental domain of `ℂ*/b^ℤ`. So the zeros of ζ sit inside a single copy of the torus, for every base at once.

decls.name: riemannHypothesis_iff_zeros_on_middle_circle
decls.why: RH, as a statement about one annulus. Every nontrivial zero lies in the fundamental annulus `b^(−1) < |z| < 1`; RH says every one of them lies on its middle circle `|z| = b^(−1/2)`, which `inversion_fixes_circle` identifies as the fixed set of `z ↦ b^(−1)/z`. The middle circle is the geometric mean of the two boundaries, and the inversion swaps those boundaries.
decls.proves: RiemannHypothesis ↔ ∀ (s : ℂ), riemannZeta s = 0 → ¬(∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * (n + 1)) → s ≠ 1 → ‖(b : ℂ) ^ (-s)‖ = b ^ (-(1 : ℝ) / 2)

decls.name: zmap_pair_product
decls.why: The pair identity. `‖z_s‖ · ‖z_{1−s}‖ = b^(−1)` for every `s`, so the geometric mean of a point and its inversion partner is always `b^(−1/2)`.

decls.name: pair_collapses_iff_critical
decls.why: The pair collapses exactly on the critical line. `‖z_s‖ = ‖z_{1−s}‖` iff `Re s = 1/2` — the two are equal only at the geometric mean their product pins.

decls.name: riemannHypothesis_iff_pair_collapses
decls.why: RH: the pair collapses at every zero. Mathlib's `RiemannHypothesis` holds exactly when each nontrivial zero has the same modulus as its inversion partner. Since `zmap_pair_product` pins their geometric mean at `b^(−1/2)` unconditionally, collapsing and landing on the middle circle are one event.
decls.proves: RiemannHypothesis ↔ ∀ (s : ℂ), riemannZeta s = 0 → ¬(∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * (n + 1)) → s ≠ 1 → ‖(b : ℂ) ^ (-s)‖ = ‖(b : ℂ) ^ (-(1 - s))‖

decls.name: sym_zero_on_outer_circle
decls.why: A zero of the table's symbol lands on `|z| = 1`.

decls.name: sym_zero_partner_on_inner_circle
decls.why: Its inversion partner lands on `|z| = b^(−1)`.

decls.name: critical_circle_is_lattice_inversion_mean
decls.why: The table's lattice, inverted, gives the critical circle. The zero comes from the table; the inversion puts it and its partner at `|z| = 1` and `|z| = b^(−1)`; their geometric mean is `b^(−1/2)`, which `on_critical_line_iff_norm` reads as `Re s = 1/2`.

header: TwinLattice — a twin pair is a lattice site, not a coincidence of spacing. Every twin pair above 3 is `(6k − 1, 6k + 1)`. The single integer between them is `6k`. So a twin pair is not two primes that happen to sit two apart: it is a site on the `2·3` lattice with primes on both shoulders, and counting twins is counting doubly-flanked lattice sites.

decls.name: twin_lower_mod_six
decls.why: The lattice. Every twin pair above 3 has its lower member at `6k − 1`. `3 < p` is not decoration: `(3,5)` is the one exception, and `three_five_exceptional` below exhibits it rather than leaving it implied.

decls.name: twin_pocket
decls.why: The pocket. The single integer between a twin pair is a multiple of 6. That is the site; the pair is what is attached to it.

decls.name: three_five_exceptional
decls.why: `(3,5)` is the exception, exhibited rather than assumed. Its pocket is 4, which is not on the lattice. It is also the first twin pair, so the lattice reading begins at `(5,7)`.

header: ZeroCells — the four zeros are one object with four names, and the kernel now says so.

decls.name: construction_eq
decls.why: The construction module's list is the computed one. `rfl`, and that is what makes it a check: edit either list and this stops compiling.

decls.name: seedPerturbation_eq
decls.why: The seed-perturbation module's list is the computed one. It was re-read independently from `imported/lattice_mapper/32bit/dyadic_difference_table_32.csv`, so this equality is also a statement that the imported table and `pi2n_cache` agree at those four cells.

decls.name: pairIdentity_eq
decls.why: The pair-identity module's list is the computed one.

decls.name: construction_all_vanish
decls.why: Every cell `Construction.measured_zeros` names vanishes — now derived, not transcribed.
decls.proves: ∀ c ∈ Construction.measured_zeros, Construction.tableFrom Zeros.dyadicRow (c.1 : ℤ) c.2 = 0

decls.name: seedPerturbation_all_vanish
decls.why: Every cell `SeedPerturbation.zero_cells` names vanishes.
decls.proves: ∀ c ∈ SeedPerturbation.zero_cells, Construction.tableFrom Zeros.dyadicRow (c.1 : ℤ) c.2 = 0

decls.name: pairIdentity_all_vanish
decls.why: Every cell `PairIdentity.zero_cells` names vanishes.
decls.proves: ∀ c ∈ PairIdentity.zero_cells, Construction.tableFrom Zeros.dyadicRow (c.1 : ℤ) c.2 = 0

decls.name: all_four_have_length_four
decls.why: All four names, one length. The "exactly four" of the papers is now a property of a single object rather than of four lists that happen to agree.

header: Zeros — what is provable about the four exact zeros, and what is not. THE MEASUREMENT (results/O16_run2.log): over r <= 62, d <= 61 the dyadic prime difference table has exactly four exact zeros — (2,1), (4,1), (8,3), (20,6) — and no others. The centered table has none at all.

decls.name: IsTable
decls.why: The table recurrence: each cell is the difference of the two above it. Depth is carried in ℕ. An earlier version quantified `d` over ℤ, which is satisfiable but not by the bench's table: `Construction.tableFrom` has type `ℤ → ℕ → ℤ` and cannot be passed at all, and the obvious `toNat` adapter makes the recurrence at `d = -1` read `N r = N r - N (r-1)`, forcing `N (r-1) = 0` at every rung. So the theorem below was quantified over a class the object it is about is not in.

decls.name: tableFrom_isTable
decls.why: The bench's table is one. The hypothesis of `zero_iff_repeat` now has a witness: it is the second conjunct of `Construction.tableFrom_isTableOf`, which itself depends on no axioms.

decls.name: zero_iff_repeat
decls.why: A zero is exactly a repeat one depth up. This is definitional, and it is the only characterisation of a zero the chain supplies.
decls.proves: f r (d + 1) = 0 ↔ f r d = f (r - 1) d

decls.name: neg_below_zero
decls.why: A zero puts its left neighbour, negated, directly beneath it. With the cell above vanishing, the recurrence has nothing to subtract from.

decls.name: pair_shares_diagonal
decls.why: And those two cells share a diagonal. The left neighbour sits at `(r-1, d)` and the copy at `(r, d+1)`, and `r - d` is the same for both. So every zero places a `±v` pair as adjacent cells on the diagonal one in -- `±343` at `(20,6)`, `±5` at `(8,3)`, both measured in `The-Fold.md` § C3.

decls.name: window_shared_of_composite_exponent
decls.why: The (8,3) window is shared. Depth 3 spans `2^4 = 4^2`, so base 4 reaches it at depth 1. Against `Zeros.window_exclusive_of_prime_exponent`, which puts base 2 alone in the (20,6) window, the two deep zeros are different kinds of object.

decls.name: measured_zeros
decls.why: The four exact zeros, `(r, d)`, over `r <= 62`, `d <= 61`. `results/O16_run2.log`. Unexplained: no theorem above predicts these — their LOCATION is not derived, and nothing here changes that.

decls.name: pi2
decls.why: `π(2^n)` for `n = 0…20`, read from `pi2n_cache.json`. This is the only measured input to anything below — 21 integers, and no other data enters.

decls.name: dyadicRow
decls.why: The depth-0 row `N(r) = π(2^r) − π(2^(r−1))`: the primes in `(2^(r−1), 2^r]`.

decls.name: zero_2_1
decls.why: `(2,1)` vanishes: `1·1 − 1·1 = 0`, computed by the kernel from `pi2`.

decls.name: zero_8_3
decls.why: `(8,3)` vanishes: `23 − 3·13 + 3·7 − 5 = 0`, four values of `π`.

decls.name: zero_20_6
decls.why: `(20,6)` vanishes: the depth-6 stencil on seven values of `π`, spanning `2^13` to `2^20`. The deep zero, computed.

decls.name: measured_zeros_all_vanish
decls.why: The list's own claim, as a theorem. Every cell `measured_zeros` names vanishes on the dyadic row.
decls.proves: ∀ c ∈ measured_zeros, Construction.tableFrom dyadicRow (c.1 : ℤ) c.2 = 0

decls.name: nonzero_7_3
decls.why: A non-zero neighbour, so the check can fail.

decls.name: nonzero_19_6
decls.why: The `+343` of `papers/The-Fold.md` § C3, the partner of the `−343` that a zero at `(20,6)` forces onto `(20,7)`.

decls.name: measured_repeat_20_6
decls.why: The repeats that produce the two deep zeros. `results/joint_dyadic_triadic_table.csv`, rows 19/20 at d5 and rows 7/8 at d2.

decls.name: measured_centered_zero_count
decls.why: The centered (skew-adjoint) table has no exact zeros at all, `r <= 62`, `d <= 30`. `results/O16_run2.log`.

decls.name: four_zeros_only
decls.why: Four zeros in 1953 cells. Recorded, not derived.

decls.name: zero_at_20_6_of_repeat
decls.why: The measured repeat gives the deep zero, through the theorem. `O27` reads `d5` at `r = 19` and `r = 20` as both 623; `zero_iff_repeat` turns that into `(20,6) = 0` without computing anything. The measurement is the input and the vanishing is the output, which is the only direction this file supports.

decls.name: zero_at_8_3_of_repeat
decls.why: The same for the other deep zero, where the repeated value is 4.

header: ZerosStencil — the Mathlib-dependent half of `Zeros.lean`. Split out of `Zeros.lean` on 2026-08-26. The classification is by axiom pin, not by subject: these are exactly the fifteen theorems whose `#print axioms` carries `Classical.choice`, and every one of them acquires it from Mathlib — `Finset.range` and the alternating-sum lemmas for the stencil family, `Nat.factorization` and `Nat.dvd_prime_pow` for the four ladder results. Notes entries 59, 66 and 187 are the record; 66 predicted this exact list two weeks bef…

decls.name: tableFrom_eq_fwdDiff
decls.why: The table's `d`-fold backward difference is `(-1)^d` times Mathlib's `d`-fold forward difference at step `-1`. The bridge exists so that `tableFrom_eq_stencil` can borrow Mathlib's binomial theorem rather than redo the index bookkeeping.
decls.proves: Construction.tableFrom N r d = (-1 : ℤ) ^ d * (fwdDiff (-1 : ℤ))^[d] N r

decls.name: stencil
decls.why: The `N`-fold alternating binomial functional — the stencil that produces a cell at depth `N-1` from `N+1` values of the counting function.

decls.name: tableFrom_eq_stencil
decls.why: The operator IS Pascal. The cell at `(r,d)` — `d` backward differences of the row — equals the alternating binomial stencil of order `d` applied to the `d+1` row values in its window.
decls.proves: Construction.tableFrom N r d = stencil d (fun k => N (r - k))

decls.name: stencil_add
decls.why: The stencil is linear in the sampled values. So a zero is a single linear equation on the `N+1` values of `pi` inside its window — one condition, hence codimension one. Nothing here says when it is satisfied.
decls.proves: stencil N (fun k => g k + h k) = stencil N g + stencil N h

decls.name: stencil_smul
decls.why: And scalars pass through — linearity's other half, beside `stencil_add`.
decls.proves: stencil N (fun k => c * g k) = c * stencil N g

decls.name: stencil_annihilates_const
decls.why: The stencil's positive and negative arms carry equal total weight. For `N = 7` each arm sums to 64: the balance is exact by construction, not by anything about the primes.

decls.name: wingPlus
decls.why: The `+` wing: the even-index arm of the stencil, unsigned.

decls.name: wingMinus
decls.why: The `−` wing: the odd-index arm, unsigned.

decls.name: stencil_eq_wings
decls.why: The fold is an identity, not a test. `cell = wing⁺ − wing⁻`, always.
decls.proves: stencil N g = wingPlus N g - wingMinus N g

decls.name: stencil_eq_zero_iff_wings
decls.why: A zero is where the wings balance.
decls.proves: stencil N g = 0 ↔ wingPlus N g = wingMinus N g

decls.name: tableFrom_eq_zero_iff_wings
decls.why: The cell, folded. Through `tableFrom_eq_stencil`: the table's cell at `(r,d)` vanishes exactly when the two wings of its window balance.
decls.proves: Construction.tableFrom N r d = 0 ↔ wingPlus d (fun k => N (r - k)) = wingMinus d (fun k => N (r - k))

decls.name: repeat_iff_wings
decls.why: Two readings of one fact. `zero_iff_repeat` says a cell vanishes iff the row repeats at the depth below. This says it vanishes iff the wings balance. The repeat reading and the fold reading are the same statement, and until now nothing in the tree connected them.
decls.proves: Construction.tableFrom N r d = Construction.tableFrom N (r - 1) d ↔ wingPlus (d + 1) (fun k => N (r - k)) = wingMinus (d + 1) (fun k => N (r - k))

decls.name: stencil_weights_antisymm
decls.why: The stencil is antisymmetric when its order is odd. Reflecting an index about the midpoint negates its weight, because `(N-k) + k = N` is odd and so the two indices have opposite parity.

decls.name: stencil_arms_eq
decls.why: The two arms weigh the same. `stencil_annihilates_const` says the signed weights cancel; written as two sums, that is the positive-index arm equalling the negative-index arm. `(1 + (-1)^k)` is twice the indicator of even `k` and `(1 - (-1)^k)` twice the indicator of odd `k`, so this is the split with the division cleared.
decls.proves: (∑ k ∈ Finset.range (N + 1), (1 + (-1 : ℤ) ^ k) * (N.choose k)) = ∑ k ∈ Finset.range (N + 1), (1 - (-1 : ℤ) ^ k) * (N.choose k)

decls.name: stencil_arm_doubled
decls.why: And each arm is `2^(N-1)`. Doubled, an arm is the whole row, `2^N`. With `stencil_arms_eq` that fixes both at half the row -- 64 and 64 at `N = 7`, 8 and 8 at `N = 4`, which is what `The-Fold.md` § B1 reports.
decls.proves: (∑ k ∈ Finset.range (N + 1), (1 + (-1 : ℤ) ^ k) * (N.choose k)) = 2 ^ N

decls.name: window_exclusive_of_prime_exponent
decls.why: The (20,6) window is base-2 exclusive. Depth 6 spans a ratio of `2^7`. Since 7 is prime, no integer base `b >= 2` reaches that window at any integer depth `k >= 2`. Base 2 at depth 6 is the only way to look through it.

decls.name: LaddersMeet
decls.why: Two ladders share a rung above `x = 1` exactly when some power of one is a power of the other. `Commensurate-Ladders.md` § A2 states the real-log form, `log b / log c` rational; this is the same condition in ℕ, which is where the rungs actually sit and which needs no transcendence.

decls.name: base_of_meets_two
decls.why: Only powers of two reach a dyadic window. If any positive power of `b` equals a power of 2, then `b` is itself a power of 2. So the ladders meeting base 2 are exactly `2, 4, 8, 16, …` and no others -- which is the general form of `window_exclusive_of_prime_exponent`, stated for every window rather than for `2^7`.

decls.name: factorization_proportional
decls.why: Two ladders that meet have proportional exponents. If some power of `b` equals some power of `c`, then at every prime the two exponents stand in the ratio `m : n`. This is the "shared lineage" of `Commensurate-Ladders.md` § A2 in exact form -- not that `b` and `c` are related somehow, but that their prime signatures are one vector scaled two ways.
decls.proves: n * b.factorization p = m * c.factorization p

decls.name: primeFactors_eq_of_meets
decls.why: And they are built from the same primes. Proportionality with both exponents nonzero forces the supports to agree, so ladders that meet are made of one prime set. Bases 2 and 3 meet nowhere above `x = 1` for exactly this reason -- there is no common ancestor because there is no common prime.

header: Abscissa — the contour's abscissa as a parameter, with RH as one instance. WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. `lean_stage3/Stage3/LineBound.lean:1091` defines

decls.name: σθ
decls.why: The parameterised abscissa. `σθ θ X = θ + 1/log X`. The existing `RHPull.σRH` is the `θ = 1/2` case.

decls.name: σθ_half
decls.why: The weld. At `θ = 1/2` this is the abscissa the built machine already uses, definitionally.

decls.name: σθ_re

header: AliasClass — block J10a of `lean_stage3/design/joints.md`. 2026-11-22. Joint 10 on the table's own ladder, first piece. On the ladder `2^r` a zero `ρ` of ζ enters only through `z = 2^ρ`: its mode at row `r` is `z^r` and its symbol is `1 − z⁻¹`. Zeros with the same `z` have the same real part and heights that differ by a multiple of `2π/log 2`; the ladder folds them together. This module proves that folding never cancels: the zeros sharing a `z` contribute to the cell one mode whose weight is not zero, at every dept…

header: Assembly — step 5, slice 1: RH meets the zero sum. The explicit formula's zero side is `Σ_{|γ|<T} m(ρ)·x^ρ/ρ`. This module defines that sum (`zeroPartialSum`), states the hEF leaf (`StmtExplicitFormula` — the truncated explicit formula with explicit remainder, the one genuinely open piece), and proves what RH does to the zero side, kernel-checked:

decls.name: re_eq_half_of_RH
decls.why: Under RH every nontrivial zero sits on the critical line. The strip membership rules out the trivial zeros and `s = 1`, so Mathlib's `RiemannHypothesis` applies directly.

decls.name: half_le_norm_of_RH
decls.why: Under RH, `|ρ| ≥ 1/2`.

decls.name: norm_cpow_of_RH
decls.why: The RH collapse: `‖x^ρ‖ = √x` for `x > 0`.

decls.name: norm_term_le_of_RH
decls.why: Each zero term is at most `2√x` in norm, from `|ρ| ≥ 1/2`.

decls.name: zeroPartialSum
decls.why: The order-weighted partial zero sum below height `T`: `Σ_{|γ|<T} m(ρ)·x^ρ/ρ`.

decls.name: StmtExplicitFormula
decls.why: The hEF leaf — the truncated explicit formula with explicit remainder. The one genuinely open analytic input of stage 3 (entry 119): every proof assistant lacks it; IEANTN targets it. Stated over Mathlib's Chebyshev `ψ` and the order-weighted partial sum.

decls.name: StmtExplicitFormulaPoly
decls.why: The `T ≤ x²`-regime form — the shape the contour proof delivers (`Glue.explicit_formula_poly`) and all the assembly consumes (`T = 2^(K+1) ≤ 2x ≤ x²`). Approved leaf-shape change (entry 271).

decls.name: norm_zeroPartialSum_le
decls.why: The zero side controlled by the count, under RH: `‖zeroPartialSum x 2^(K+1)‖ ≤ 2√x·(2|N(2^(K+1))| + W)`, through IEANTN's sorry-free `weighted_cumulative_count_le`. With ZeroSum's `N_abs_le` this is `√x`·(T·log T)-arithmetic under hNT.
decls.proves: ‖zeroPartialSum x ((2 : ℝ) ^ (K + 1))‖ ≤ 2 * Real.sqrt x * (2 * |riemannZeta.N ((2 : ℝ) ^ (K + 1))| + weightedZeroHeightBucket)

decls.name: inv_le_dyadic_sum
decls.why: Scalar dyadic domination: for `1 ≤ γ < 2^(K+1)`, `γ⁻¹ ≤ Σ_{j≤K} (2^j)⁻¹·[γ < 2^(j+1)]` — the largest surviving indicator sits at the shell containing `γ`, and its weight already dominates.
decls.proves: ∀ γ : ℝ, 1 ≤ γ → γ < 2 ^ (K + 1) → γ⁻¹ ≤ ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (K + 1), ((2 : ℝ) ^ j)⁻¹ * (if γ < 2 ^ (j + 1) then 1 else 0)

decls.name: norm_term_le_dyadic
decls.why: Each zero term is dominated by the dyadic indicator weights: `‖x^ρ/ρ‖ ≤ 2√x·Σ_{j≤K} (2^j)⁻¹·[|γ| < 2^(j+1)]` for `|γ| < 2^(K+1)`.
decls.proves: ‖(x : ℂ) ^ (ρ : ℂ) / (ρ : ℂ)‖ ≤ 2 * Real.sqrt x * ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (K + 1), ((2 : ℝ) ^ j)⁻¹ * (if |(ρ : ℂ).im| < 2 ^ (j + 1) then 1 else 0)

decls.name: norm_zeroPartialSum_le_sharp
decls.why: The sharp zero-side bound, dyadic form. Under RH, the zero side is controlled level by level: each level's weighted count enters through IEANTN's sorry-free `weighted_cumulative_count_le`, reached by the scalar domination — no shell partition anywhere.
decls.proves: ‖zeroPartialSum x ((2 : ℝ) ^ (K + 1))‖ ≤ 2 * Real.sqrt x * ∑ j ∈ Finset.range (K + 1), ((2 : ℝ) ^ j)⁻¹ * (2 * |riemannZeta.N ((2 : ℝ) ^ (j + 1))| + weightedZeroHeightBucket)

decls.name: norm_zeroPartialSum_le_logsq
decls.why: The zero side at `√x·(log T)²`, under RH + hNT — the sharp form. Combining the dyadic bound with ZeroSum's counting arithmetic: with `T = 2^(K+1)`, the zero side is at most `2√x·(2·[(log 2/2π)(K+1)(K+2) + 3(K+1)/π + 2(RvM(T) + 7/8)] + 2W)`.
decls.proves: ‖zeroPartialSum x ((2 : ℝ) ^ (K + 1))‖ ≤ 2 * Real.sqrt x * (2 * (Real.log 2 / (2 * Real.pi) * (K + 1) * (K + 2) + 3 * (K + 1) / Real.pi + 2 * (riemannZeta.RvM b₁ b₂ b₃ ((2 : ℝ) ^ (K + 1)) + 7 / 8)) + 2 * weightedZeroHeightBucket)

decls.name: rem_arith
decls.why: Scalar arithmetic of the remainder: `x ≤ T`, `0 ≤ G ≤ 3L`, `1 ≤ L` give `c₁·x·G²/T + c₂·L ≤ (9c₁+c₂)·L²`.
decls.proves: c₁ * xx * G ^ 2 / TT + c₂ * L ≤ (9 * c₁ + c₂) * L ^ 2

decls.name: zeroinner_arith
decls.why: Scalar arithmetic of the zero side's inner factor: the dyadic level bounds and the RvM bound turn the `(K, RvM)` expression into `2·(7+4b₁+4b₂+2b₃)·L² + 2W`.
needs: hR : R ≤ (2 * b₁ + 2 * b₂ + b₃) * L ^ 2

decls.name: assembly_arith
decls.why: Scalar arithmetic of the final absorption into `C·S·L²`.

decls.name: psiWeak_of_RH_EF_NT
decls.why: THE ASSEMBLY — the decomposition closed. Under hRH (Mathlib's `RiemannHypothesis`), hEF (`StmtExplicitFormula c₁ c₂ x₁` — the truncated explicit formula, the open leaf), and hNT (`Riemann_vonMangoldt_bound b₁ b₂ b₃` — Rosser Th. 19, the other open leaf), the ψ-side weak bound holds with computed constant: `StmtPsiWeak (9c₁ + c₂ + 28 + 16b₁ + 16b₂ + 8b₃ + 4W) 2 (max x₁ 16)`. The dyadic level is chosen from `x` itself (`K = Nat.log 2 ⌊x⌋`, so `x < 2^(K+1) ≤ 2x`). PsiToPi's `schoenfeldWeak_of_psiWeak` carries the conclusion to `π − Li`, Statement's `weakWindow_of_global` to the window, O68's arit…
decls.proves: StmtPsiWeak (9 * c₁ + c₂ + 28 + 16 * b₁ + 16 * b₂ + 8 * b₃ + 4 * W) 2 (max x₁ 16)

decls.name: residue_rectangle_multi
decls.why: The multi-pole residue theorem on a rectangle. If `f` agrees off the pole set with `g + Σ_p A p/(s − p)` for `g` holomorphic on the whole rectangle and every pole interior, then the rectangle integral of `f` collects every residue.
needs: pIn : ∀ p ∈ P, Rectangle z w ∈ nhds p
principal : Set.EqOn (f - fun s ↦ ∑ p ∈ P, A p / (s - p)) g (Rectangle z w \ (P : Set ℂ))
decls.proves: RectangleIntegral' f z w = ∑ p ∈ P, A p

decls.name: residue_rectangle_of_local
decls.why: The residue theorem from local data. `f` holomorphic on the rectangle off a finite interior pole set, and at each pole `p` equal to `(analytic at p) + A p/(s − p)` on a punctured neighborhood: the rectangle integral collects every residue. The global extension is glued from the local analytic parts.
needs: pIn : ∀ p ∈ P, Rectangle z w ∈ nhds p
fHolo : HolomorphicOn f (Rectangle z w \ (P : Set ℂ))
hloc : ∀ p ∈ P, ∃ h : ℂ → ℂ, AnalyticAt ℂ h p ∧ ∀ᶠ s in nhdsWithin p {p}ᶜ, f s = h s + A p / (s - p)
decls.proves: RectangleIntegral' f z w = ∑ p ∈ P, A p

decls.name: analyticAt_dslope
decls.why: `dslope` of an analytic function is analytic at the point.

decls.name: div_sub_eq_dslope
decls.why: Off the point, `f s/(s−p)` splits as `f p/(s−p) + dslope f p s`.
decls.proves: f s / (s - p) = f p / (s - p) + dslope f p s

decls.name: zeta_local_data
decls.why: The local pole data of `G = (−ζ′/ζ)·x^s/s` at a factorization point. Where `ζ` factors as `(s−p)^n·g` with `g` analytic and nonvanishing at `p ≠ 0`, `G` splits as `analytic + (−n·x^p/p)/(s−p)` on a punctured neighborhood: the pole is simple with residue `−n·x^p/p`. Covers every nontrivial zero (`n = order ≥ 1`) and the pole of `ζ` at `1` (`n = −1`, residue `+x`) in one statement.
needs: hfac : ∀ᶠ s in nhdsWithin p {p}ᶜ, riemannZeta s = (s - p) ^ n * g s
decls.proves: ∃ h : ℂ → ℂ, AnalyticAt ℂ h p ∧ ∀ᶠ s in nhdsWithin p {p}ᶜ, - deriv riemannZeta s / riemannZeta s * ((x:ℝ):ℂ) ^ s / s = h s + (-(n:ℂ) * ((x:ℝ):ℂ) ^ p / p) / (s - p)

decls.name: zeta_order_ne_top
decls.why: The order of `ζ` at any point off the pole is finite (identity theorem on `ℂ∖{1}`, as in `one_le_zeta_order`).

decls.name: zeta_local_data_zero
decls.why: Local pole data of `G` at a nontrivial zero: residue `−(order)·x^ρ/ρ`.
decls.proves: ∃ h : ℂ → ℂ, AnalyticAt ℂ h ρ ∧ ∀ᶠ s in nhdsWithin ρ {ρ}ᶜ, - deriv riemannZeta s / riemannZeta s * ((x:ℝ):ℂ) ^ s / s = h s + (-(analyticOrderNatAt riemannZeta ρ : ℂ) * ((x:ℝ):ℂ) ^ ρ / ρ) / (s - ρ)

decls.name: zeta_local_data_one
decls.why: Local pole data of `G` at `1`: residue `+x`. The factorization `ζ = (s−1)^{−1}·g` is built from the completed zeta function.
decls.proves: ∃ h : ℂ → ℂ, AnalyticAt ℂ h 1 ∧ ∀ᶠ s in nhdsWithin 1 {1}ᶜ, - deriv riemannZeta s / riemannZeta s * ((x:ℝ):ℂ) ^ s / s = h s + ((x:ℝ):ℂ) / (s - 1)

decls.name: zeta_local_data_origin
decls.why: Local pole data of `G` at `0`: residue `−ζ′(0)/ζ(0)`.
decls.proves: ∃ h : ℂ → ℂ, AnalyticAt ℂ h 0 ∧ ∀ᶠ s in nhdsWithin 0 {0}ᶜ, - deriv riemannZeta s / riemannZeta s * ((x:ℝ):ℂ) ^ s / s = h s + (- deriv riemannZeta 0 / riemannZeta 0) / (s - 0)

decls.name: zeta_ne_zero_of_re_mem
decls.why: No zeros on the strip `re ∈ [−1, 0]`: the functional equation carries nonvanishing over from `re ∈ [1, 2]`. The cosine factor can only vanish at `s = 1`, where `ζ` has its pole instead.

decls.name: sq_mul_zeta_analyticAt_one
decls.why: `(s−1)²·ζ` is analytic at `1`, from the unconditional completed-zeta formula (junk values at `s = 1` agree on both sides).

decls.name: zeta_meromorphicOn
decls.why: `ζ` is meromorphic on any set.

decls.name: zeta_zeros_rectangle_finite
decls.why: The zeros of `ζ` in a closed rectangle form a finite set.
decls.proves: {ρ : ℂ | riemannZeta ρ = 0 ∧ ρ ∈ Rectangle z w}.Finite

decls.name: order_bridge
decls.why: The ledger's `riemannZeta.order` agrees with `analyticOrderNatAt` away from the pole (mirrors PNT+ KadiriZeroCounting's own bridge).
decls.proves: ((riemannZeta.order ρ : ℤ) : ℂ) = ((analyticOrderNatAt riemannZeta ρ : ℕ) : ℂ)

decls.name: zeroPartialSum_eq_sum
decls.why: `zeroPartialSum` as a concrete finite sum, over any `Finset` enumerating exactly the nontrivial zeros below the height.
needs: hiff : ∀ ρ : ℂ, ρ ∈ ZF ↔ (ρ ∈ Kadiri.NontrivialZeros ∧ |ρ.im| < T')
decls.proves: Stage3.zeroPartialSum x T' = ∑ p ∈ ZF, ((analyticOrderNatAt riemannZeta p : ℂ) * ((x : ℂ) ^ p / p))

decls.name: analyticAt_conj_conj
decls.why: Analyticity transports through conjugation: `conj ∘ g ∘ conj` is analytic at `conj p`.
decls.proves: AnalyticAt ℂ (fun w ↦ (starRingEnd ℂ) (g ((starRingEnd ℂ) w))) ((starRingEnd ℂ) p)

decls.name: zeta_order_conj
decls.why: The order of `ζ` at the conjugate of a point equals the order at the point (`ζ(conj s) = conj ζ(s)`).
decls.proves: analyticOrderNatAt riemannZeta ((starRingEnd ℂ) ρ) = analyticOrderNatAt riemannZeta ρ

decls.name: zeta_order_reflect
decls.why: The reflection-order lemma: the order of `ζ` at `1 − conj ρ` equals the order at `ρ`, on the open strip — the functional equation's factor is analytic and nonvanishing there.
decls.proves: analyticOrderNatAt riemannZeta (1 - (starRingEnd ℂ) ρ) = analyticOrderNatAt riemannZeta ρ

decls.name: residue_identity
decls.why: Slice 4 — the residue identity on the good rectangle. The zeros enter here: pulling the line integral to `σ = −1` collects the pole at `1` (residue `x`), the pole at `0` (residue `−ζ′/ζ(0)`), and every nontrivial zero below height `T'` (residue `−m_ρ·x^ρ/ρ`).
needs: hgood : ∀ ρ : ℂ, riemannZeta ρ = 0 → 0 < ρ.re → zeroGap T ≤ |ρ.im - T'|
decls.proves: RectangleIntegral' (fun s : ℂ ↦ (- deriv riemannZeta s / riemannZeta s) * ((x:ℝ):ℂ) ^ s / s) (((-1/4 : ℝ):ℂ) - Complex.I * T') (((1 + 1/Real.log x : ℝ):ℂ) + Complex.I * T') = (x : ℂ) - deriv riemannZeta 0 / riemannZeta 0 - Stage3.zeroPartialSum x T'

header: # S3 — the edge bound (FinalBound rescale + gap-eating) The Landau partial fraction transported from PNT+'s normalized `FinalBound` (unit ball) to the ball at `3/2 + iT′`, for `g = (s−1)²·ζ` (entire; the pole cleared, one extra order-1 zero at `1`). Inputs: `ZetaGrowth.sq_zeta_band_bound` (the B), PNT+'s `ZetaFixedLowerBound` (the f(0)), `ContourShift`'s good heights, fences, and reflection-order (the eating).

decls.name: c0
decls.why: The ball center at height `T′`.

decls.name: gz
decls.why: `g = (s−1)²·ζ` — entire, zeros = ζ-zeros plus an order-1 zero at 1.

decls.name: gz_lower
decls.why: The explicit lower bound at the center.

decls.name: zeta_ratio_pos
decls.why: The lower-bound constant is positive.

decls.name: gz_c0_ne
decls.why: The center's value is nonzero.

decls.name: gz_zero_cases
decls.why: A `gz`-zero is `1` or a `ζ`-zero.

decls.name: gz_zeros_ball_finite
decls.why: The `gz`-zeros in any ball around the center are finite.
decls.proves: {w : ℂ | gz w = 0 ∧ ‖w - c0 T'‖ ≤ ρ}.Finite

decls.name: gz_partial_fraction
decls.why: The rescaled Landau partial fraction. At any height `T′ ≥ 2` and any `u` on the segment `re ∈ [−1/4, 2]` at that height that is not a `gz`-zero, the log-derivative of `gz` minus the simple-pole sum over `gz`-zeros within `46/25` of the center is `≤ C·log T′`. Transported from PNT+'s normalized `FinalBound` with radii `22/25 < 23/25 < 19/20 < 49/50`.
decls.proves: ∃ C : ℝ, 0 < C ∧ ∀ T' : ℝ, 2 ≤ T' → ∀ u : ℂ, u.im = T' → -1/4 ≤ u.re → u.re ≤ 2 → gz u ≠ 0 → ‖deriv gz u / gz u - ∑ w ∈ (gz_zeros_ball_finite T' (by norm_num : (0:ℝ) ≤ 46/25)).toFinset, (analyticOrderNatAt gz w : ℂ) / (u - w)‖ ≤ C * Real.log T'

decls.name: gz_order_eq
decls.why: Away from `1`, the order of `gz` is the order of `ζ` — the factor `(s−1)²` carries order zero there.
decls.proves: analyticOrderNatAt gz w = analyticOrderNatAt riemannZeta w

decls.name: ball_zero_shape
decls.why: Every ball zero at heights `≥ 2` is a `ζ`-zero on the open strip, with ordinate within `46/25` of `T′`.

decls.name: ball_order_sum_le
decls.why: The ball order-count: the total multiplicity of `gz`-zeros in the `46/25`-ball at height `T′` is `≤ C·log T′` — four Jensen windows for `T′ ≥ 4` with the reflection charging left-zeros to partners, and a fixed-rectangle constant for `T′ < 4`.
decls.proves: ∃ C : ℝ, 0 < C ∧ ∀ T' : ℝ, 2 ≤ T' → (∑ w ∈ (gz_zeros_ball_finite T' (by norm_num : (0:ℝ) ≤ 46/25)).toFinset, (analyticOrderNatAt gz w : ℝ)) ≤ C * Real.log T'

decls.name: gz_logderiv
decls.why: The log-derivative identity: `gz′/gz = 2/(s−1) + ζ′/ζ` away from the pole and the zeros.
decls.proves: deriv gz u / gz u = 2/(u - 1) + deriv riemannZeta u / riemannZeta u

decls.name: deriv_zeta_conj
decls.why: Conjugation transfers the derivative of `ζ`.
decls.proves: deriv riemannZeta ((starRingEnd ℂ) s) = (starRingEnd ℂ) (deriv riemannZeta s)

decls.name: edge_bound_core
decls.why: The pointwise edge bound, unified. For `u` on the band `re ∈ [−1/4, 2]` at height `t ≥ 2`, with a lower bound `δ ≤ 1` on the distance from `u` to every ball zero: `‖ζ′/ζ(u)‖ ≤ C·(log t)/δ + C·log t`. Both edges specialize this: the left edge with `δ = 1/4`, the good horizontals with `δ = zeroGap T`.
decls.proves: ∃ C : ℝ, 0 < C ∧ ∀ t : ℝ, 2 ≤ t → ∀ u : ℂ, u.im = t → -1/4 ≤ u.re → u.re ≤ 2 → riemannZeta u ≠ 0 → ∀ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ → δ ≤ 1 → (∀ w ∈ (gz_zeros_ball_finite t (by norm_num : (0:ℝ) ≤ 46/25)).toFinset, δ ≤ ‖u - w‖) → ‖deriv riemannZeta u / riemannZeta u‖ ≤ C * Real.log t / δ

header: ExplicitBump — a concrete `ν`, so `mellin_bump_bounded`'s `B` is a numeral. WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. `RHPull.psi_weak_of_RH` (`Stage3/LineBound.lean:2357`) assembles its constant from four distinct existentials:

decls.name: sqPos_eq
decls.why: `(max 0 u)²` written without the max, for differentiation.
decls.proves: (max 0 u) ^ 2 = if u ≤ 0 then 0 else u ^ 2

decls.name: hasDerivAt_sqPos
decls.why: The derivative of `(max 0 ·)²` is `2·max 0 ·`, everywhere — including at the join, where both one-sided derivatives vanish.
decls.proves: HasDerivAt (fun t : ℝ => (max 0 t) ^ 2) (2 * max 0 u) u

decls.name: bumpP
decls.why: The interval polynomial: `p x = (x − 1/2)(2 − x)`, positive exactly on `Ioo (1/2) 2`.

decls.name: bumpC
decls.why: The normalising constant `c = 1 / ∫_{1/2}^{2} p²/x`, in closed form. `∫ p²/x = 33/16 − (3/2)·log 2`.

decls.name: bump
decls.why: The explicit bump. `C¹`, supported exactly on `Icc (1/2) 2`, non-negative, and normalised so `∫ ν(x)/x dx = 1`.

decls.name: bumpC_pos
decls.why: `∫ p²/x` is positive, so `bumpC` is well defined and positive.

decls.name: bump_support
decls.why: Support. Off `Icc (1/2) 2` the polynomial is non-positive, so the positive part is zero.

decls.name: bump_contDiff
decls.why: `C¹`. The polynomial is smooth and the positive-part square is `C¹`, so the composite is.

decls.name: bumpP_le
decls.why: `p` peaks at `x = 5/4` with value `9/16`.

decls.name: bump_le
decls.why: The sup of the bump, at the peak: `sup ν = c·(9/16)²`.

decls.name: bump_le_numeral
decls.why: The numeral. `sup ν ≤ 1.4757`, hence `mellin_bump_bounded`'s `B = 3·sup‖ν‖ + 1 ≤ 5.4271`. Both bounds are decimal, so a consumer can carry them arithmetically.

header: JensenCount — `StmtLocalCount` discharged: the Backlund-style local zero count for `ζ`, with explicit constants.

decls.name: zeta_disk_upper
decls.why: The majorant on the wide disk. `‖ζ w‖ ≤ 28 T` for `T ≥ 2` and `‖w - (2 + iT)‖ ≤ 15/8`; this is the `R = 15/16` radius of the Jensen step pulled back through `s = 2z + (2 + iT)`. On that disk `Re w ≥ 1/8 > 0` and `Im w ≥ T - 15/8 ≥ 1/8`, so the pole at `s = 1` is avoided with room.

decls.name: zeta_centre_ne_zero
decls.why: The centre `2 + iT` has real part `2`, hence `ζ` does not vanish there.

decls.name: pole_away
decls.why: The pole stays outside the mapped ball. For `T ≥ 2` and `‖z‖ ≤ 11/10`, the point `2z + (2 + iT)` is never the pole `s = 1`.

decls.name: pole_away_centre
decls.why: The pole stays outside the window. For `T ≥ 2`, every point within `11/5` of `2 + iT` differs from `1`.

decls.name: zetaWindowTwo_finite
decls.why: `ζ` has finitely many zeros within `2` of the centre.

decls.name: zetaWindow
decls.why: The window. `ζ`'s zeros in the closed disk of radius `7/4` about `2 + iT`. On the critical line this disk covers `|γ - T| ≤ √(13/16)` ≈ `0.901`, an interval of positive length — which is what radius `3/2` fails to do, being tangent to the line and so catching only `γ = T`.

decls.name: jensenF
decls.why: The normalised local model. `f z = ζ (2z + 2 + iT) / ζ (2 + iT)`; the closed unit ball maps onto `|s - (2+iT)| ≤ 2`.

decls.name: zeta_comp_analytic
decls.proves: AnalyticAt ℂ (fun z : ℂ => ζ (2 * z + (2 + Complex.I * (T : ℂ)))) w

decls.name: analyticOrderNatAt_fun_comp_affine
decls.why: The analytic order is unchanged by an invertible affine change of variable.
decls.proves: analyticOrderNatAt (fun w : ℂ => g (a * w + b)) z = analyticOrderNatAt g (a * z + b)

decls.name: jensenF_order
decls.proves: analyticOrderNatAt (jensenF T) w = analyticOrderNatAt ζ (2 * w + (2 + Complex.I * (T : ℂ)))

decls.name: zeta_local_zero_count
decls.why: THE LOCAL ZERO COUNT. For every `T ≥ 2`, the total order of the zeros of `ζ` in the closed disk `|s - (2 + iT)| ≤ 7/4` — a disk which meets the critical line in the segment `|γ - T| ≤ √(13/16)` — is at most `15 log T + 73`.
decls.proves: ∑ ρ ∈ (zetaWindow_finite hT).toFinset, (analyticOrderNatAt ζ ρ : ℝ) ≤ 15 * Real.log T + 73

decls.name: zetaLocalCount
decls.why: The count function. Total zero order of `ζ` in `|s - (2+iT)| ≤ 7/4`.

decls.name: zetaLocalCount_eq
decls.proves: zetaLocalCount T = ∑ ρ ∈ (zetaWindow_finite hT).toFinset, (analyticOrderNatAt ζ ρ : ℝ)

decls.name: localCount_holds
decls.why: THE LEAF, DISCHARGED. `StmtLocalCount` holds for the concrete zeta zero count with the explicit constants `A₁ = 15`, `A₃ = 73`. Entry 130's budget accepts `A₁ ≤ 100`, `A₃ ≤ 1000`, so these clear it with room; the widening from radius `3/2` to `7/4` cost roughly a factor of two in `A₁` and is paid out of that budget.

header: LadderFading — block J10b of `lean_stage3/design/joints.md`. 2026-11-22. Joint 10 on the table's own ladder, second piece. `AliasClass` showed that the zeros the ladder folds together contribute one mode with a weight that is not zero. This module shows that finitely many such modes of one size cannot fade: their sum along the rows is not small against that size. The proof is the table's own operation: one difference with the symbol of a mode removes that mode and keeps every other weight nonzero.
